nameStory: Hare's-ear mustard gets its curious name from its distinctive leaves that clasp around the stem, creating ear-like shapes that reminded early botanists of a rabbit's ears. The leaves wrap around the stem at their base in such a way that they form little pockets or 'ears' along the plant's length.
description: Hare's-ear mustard is a weedy annual plant in the mustard family that grows as a single, unbranched stem reaching 1-2 feet tall. It's an invasive species from Europe and Asia that has spread across North America. The plant is most notable for its thick, waxy blue-green leaves that wrap around the stem and its small yellow flowers that develop into long, beaded seed pods.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, waxy leaves up to 3.5 inches long that feel smooth and somewhat succulent to the touch. They're oval-shaped and clasp completely around the stem at their base, creating distinctive ear-like pockets.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small yellow flowers about 1/3 inch long with four petals that have narrow, claw-like bases. The flowers are tucked between pointed green sepals and bloom along the upper stem.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a single, unbranched, erect stem that feels sturdy and somewhat thick. The whole plant has a distinctive blue-green or gray-green color that stands out from other weeds.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Long, narrow seed pods (siliques) up to 5 inches long that look beaded or segmented, like a string of tiny green sausages. They point upward along the stem when mature.

habitat: Look for hare's-ear mustard in disturbed soils, roadsides, agricultural fields, and waste areas throughout New England, though it's quite rare in our region. It prefers sunny locations with well-drained soil and often appears in areas where the ground has been recently disturbed. This weedy species is much more common in the western parts of North America.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge and develop their characteristic clasping leaves. Early flowers may begin to appear in late spring on the upper stem.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with small yellow flowers opening along the stem. Long seed pods begin forming and developing their distinctive beaded appearance.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods mature and split open to release seeds. The annual plant completes its life cycle and dies back.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts remain as this is an annual plant. Seeds overwinter in the soil to germinate the following spring.

funFact: This innocent-looking mustard is actually toxic to livestock and can poison cattle, sheep, and horses if they eat too much of it, earning it the nickname 'treacle mustard' in some farming communities where it's considered a serious agricultural pest.
confusionNotes: The clasping, waxy leaves make this plant quite distinctive among mustards. Other mustards in New England typically have more divided or toothed leaves that don't wrap around the stem so completely. The blue-green color and single unbranched stem also help set it apart from most common mustard weeds.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being in the mustard family, hare's-ear mustard is toxic unlike many of its edible relatives such as watercress or garlic mustard. This plant is considered a noxious weed in many western states and provinces, though it remains very uncommon in New England.
compareHints: Hare's-ear mustard is the only species in its genus (Conringia) found in North America. Compared to other mustard family members in New England, it's unique for its completely smooth, waxy leaves that fully clasp the stem, its unbranched growth habit, and its blue-green coloration. Most other mustards have more divided leaves and branch more freely.
